utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please be seated. Good morning, ladies and gentlemen; good morning to the technical booth and the interpreters; good morning to the legal assistants and the registrar; good morning to the Prosecution and Defence counsel and the accused, whom I see are all here. We're going to take up where we left off yesterday. With respect to the question raised yesterday by the Defence counsel of Mr. Prcac, I personally have spoken to Mr. Marc Dubuisson, who is going to give us some information, maybe before the break even, on the remarks made yesterday. So that is what the Chamber can do. As you know, that is something that the registrar -- comes under the competence of the registrar, and I'm sure that Mr. Jovan Simic has taken note of that, but I give him the floor now for additional information.

utterances.speaker: MR. J. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour. I wanted, unfortunately, to inform you that the situation with respect to the medication of Mr. Prcac has remained unchanged. He has received some medicines, but they are not the kind he's used to taking. The Defence has spoken to Mr. Dubuisson, who has promised in his turn that he will bring the medicaments in by noon. I have also spoken to Mr. Prcac, and he said that he will do his best to attend the trial, as he has done from the beginning. But I should like to appeal to the Registry and the Chamber to see to this. If the problem are the medicaments, then the Defence counsel can bring his medicines in. But this can lead to a problem because his lower blood pressure is very high, which, as you know, is dangerous and could lead to an interruption of the trial through no fault of the Defence counsel and the accused, who are doing everything in their power to see that the trial goes ahead according to procedure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Jovan Simic. I think we should really get to the bottom of this to know what is going on and to hear the advice of the physician. I know we all have a certain tendency to act as physicians, but I think we ought to get to the bottom of the problem, to see the prescriptions that have been given and what medicaments are to be taken and to ensure that they should be taken so that is precisely the reason why I myself have taken certain steps, which coincide with your own, might I add. Let us now take up where we left off yesterday. Yes. Mr. Stojanovic is on his legs, I see.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour. Thank you for giving me the floor. Before we go on to the cross-examination, I should like to make an objection. I will mention the contents, however, of a confidential document. I don't know whether this, therefore, requires a private session, closed session -- does it? -- for me to disclose this information?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Has the question to do with the cross-examination of the witness, Mr. Stojanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, indeed, Your Honour. It refers to yesterday's testimony by the witness in its entirety.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I heard mention of Witness E.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, it is Witness J, Your Honour, yesterday's witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you very much. We're now going to go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Witness J. Have you had a good rest, Witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me just remind you that you are still under an oath. Today you will be answering questions that will be put to you by the Defence counsel. They will introduce themselves to you. Mr. O'Sullivan, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Witness, my name is Eugene O'Sullivan, and I'm a lawyer from Canada. Witness, you testified that you were at Omarska from June 9th until August 3rd; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And you say that you observed the organisation of personnel and the functions people fulfilled in Omarska, and you drew certain conclusions; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: You observed that there was a guard shift that came on duty at approximately 7.00 or 8.00 in the morning and was replaced by another guard shift at approximately 7.00 or 8.00 in the evening. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, I said that the first shift would arrive at the time you indicated and that they would stay until sometime in the afternoon, but I cannot be more precise as to the time. I cannot tell you the exact hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Based on your observations, there were two guard shifts, correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that there were three shifts.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Based on your observations, Witness, the shift commanders were Mladjo Radic, known as Krkan, and Gruban, known as Ckalja. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: And the third one, Milojica Kos, called Krle.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: I'll ask the assistance of the usher to show these documents to the Prosecution and then place them before the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Witness, you have two documents in front of you. One is in English and one is in Bosnian. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: The Bosnian version is a translation of the English document, and they're both in front of you so that you can refer, from time to time, to both, and I'll ask you some questions about that. Now, this is the statement you gave to the Prosecutor in 1995, and can you take the English version, and in the bottom right-hand corner of the front page, you see your signature, don't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Now, keeping with the English version -- this document is 18 pages long -- and if you'd quickly look through the bottom right-hand corner of every page, you will see your initials there; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Before you signed this statement, it was read back to you in Bosnian by the interpreter who was present during the interview; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And again looking at the English statement, on page 17. Could you turn to page 17 of the English statement. On page 17 you see your signature?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And the date on which you signed it, which is 14 February 1995.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Now, for your benefit, perhaps you could look at the front page of the Bosnian translation. The cover page of the Bosnian. It's correct that the interview was conducted on the 11th and the 14th of February, 1995?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: On the 11th of February, do you recall for how long you met with the Prosecution? Approximately.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really couldn't tell you that, but it took awhile. But I cannot be more precise than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: So it would be fair to say that it was a full day with normal breaks?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And the same is true for the second day, on February 14th?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: You were interviewed by two persons?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: You gave this statement voluntarily?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: No pressure was put on you to make this statement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: None whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And you spoke freely when you gave answers to questions?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: Completely freely.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And the events you talk about in your statement were fresher in your mind in 1995 than they are today; do you agree?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are certain events that I could never forget. Some of them are as fresh today as they were then.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And in 1995, you gave the best recollection of the most important events, places, and people, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And you told the truth in 1995?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I told the truth as I've been telling it yesterday and today.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Can I ask you to turn to page 6 of the Bosnian version, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And for those following in English, it's page 6 also. And in the English version, for those following in English, it's page -- I'll begin in the second paragraph of page 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: I'm going to read something to you, Witness, from page 6 of your statement, second paragraph. You said, I quote, "There were two guard shifts at the camp. The first shift was on duty at 7 or 8 a.m. until 7 p.m. or 8 p.m., then the second shift came on duty." I'd like to read the beginning of the following paragraph to you. "The shift commanders were Mladjo Radic, nicknamed Krkan; and a man nicknamed Ckalja, whose last name was Gruban." My question is this: Were you truthful and complete when you said this in your statement in 1995?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that, and I abide by that, but I haven't provided you with all the details. I could be sitting here for days and talk to you about what I was going through during those two months. I never have enough time to tell the whole story.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Witness, is it correct that, based on your observations, you concluded that Krle was a guard and not a shift commander?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: Krle was a shift leader.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Can I ask you to turn to page 7 of the Bosnian version of your statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And for those following in English, it's page 7 also. In English, it's the second paragraph, the second last paragraph on page 7 in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Witness, look at the fifth paragraph of page 7. Let me read you something. "I remember a guard called Krle whose full name was Milojica Kos. I knew his name because he told me his name. I learned his nickname from the guards who always referred to him as Krle. I do not remember which shift he usually worked on." My question is this: Were you telling the truth when you said that in 1995?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Witness, in the evening when you went upstairs to the sleeping room, that usually occurred around 7.00, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: Around 7.00 or 8.00. There wasn't any rule to that effect when the guards would come to the room and when they told us that they were free, and that when they were ready to escort us, at that point we would go. But there was not a particular rule about that and not a particular time.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: But it was normally between 7 and 8 p.m.; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most frequently, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Now, the night that Silvije Saric and Abdulah Puskar were beaten, you went upstairs to your sleeping room at the usual time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whether it was at the usual time or an hour or two hours later, I don't know. I cannot tell you exactly the time when I left that night, but it was around the usual time in the evening. I don't know exactly what time it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And the incident involving Saric and Puskar occurred about 11 p.m., correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, approximately. Around 11.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And it's correct that Zivko Marmat called for Saric and Puskar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: When you heard Marmat call these men, you did not see Krle, did you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see Marmat, either, because I was not allowed to leave the room. There wasn't any chance of my leaving the room, nor did I dare to.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: You did not hear Krle, did you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did hear Krle's voice very clearly.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: You did not hear anybody say Krle's name?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. Krle, the nickname. Not the name, but the nickname.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Witness, you did not know if Krle was present when Saric and Puskar were beaten, do you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not see it. I have told you that.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: You do not know if he was present.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't know for sure because I didn't see it, but according to the voices, to the names, according to the names that were being called out, I came to that conclusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Can I ask you to turn to page 13 of the Bosnian version of your statement.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise, let me just go back to this previous issue for a while. Yesterday in my testimony I said very clearly that somebody had opened the door of our room.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Would you turn to page 13 of the Bosnian document.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And for those following in English, it's page 14. In English it's page 14, the first paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And, Witness, in Bosnian, it's page 13, the third full paragraph. Let me read this to you. "There was another incident that occurred at night. Krle, Zivko Marmat, and Zdravko Govedar were on duty that night. I saw these three guards when I went upstairs to my sleeping room. Later, I heard Zivko Marmat call for Silvije Saric and Abdulah Puskar. I recognised Zivko's voice because he worked in the camp every day, and I heard his voice every day. I believe the two names were called together. I heard footsteps in the hallway. It sounded like the footsteps and voices went to a room on the left side of the hallway, which is our side of the hallway. After that I heard what I thought were sounds of blows; I don't know how to describe that. Then someone, I don't know who, came to our door and opened it slightly. We then heard loud noises, like a person being hit. Then I heard voices saying, `Please don't do this. Please let us go.' This seemed to go on forever. Later I heard footsteps in the corridor." My question is this, Witness: Is this a truthful and complete account of this event as you recalled it in 1995?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is truthful but it is not complete.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Is there any reason why you weren't complete in 1995?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: There wasn't any particular reason. It would have gone on forever. I wanted to tell them as much as I could about various events.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Did anyone stop you from telling about this event?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, nobody did.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Witness, you testified about a man named Grabovac, known as Captain. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: He wore a JNA uniform with gold on his epaulettes, correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And he was in Omarska for about ten days?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: More or less, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And you know that he was not a guard or an inspector; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: No further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. O'Sullivan. Mr. Simic, Krstan Simic, your witness. Mr. Simic, your witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: Witness J, my name is Krstan Simic. I'm an attorney from Banja Luka. I should like, in connection with your testimony and statements and appearances in the media and at international conferences, to ask several questions, and, of course, linked to your stay in Omarska. You said yesterday that you were brought to Omarska on the 9th of June, 1992, at about 10.00. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: You also said that after being taken out of the vehicle, that you were taken to a room on the top floor used by the security service. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: Would you describe for us the room you were taken to? Could you tell us how big it is? Approximately. Roughly.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: That room is located, when you go in --

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: I know that, Witness. I just asked you --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is on the right-hand side. I just want to get the image correct in my mind, if I may. So it was located on the right-hand side. First of all, there was a bathroom, a WC, and then that room. I truly couldn't tell you the surface area of the room -- I'm not good with numbers and that kind of thing -- but it was a medium-sized room. I really couldn't give you the area. I would go wrong, I'm sure, if I were to attempt to do so. There were tables as are usually found in a workplace, television, telephone, some paper, but I can't tell you how big the room was. I wouldn't like to guess. But as I said, it was a medium-sized room. There were quite a few chairs inside, several tables.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: In addition to the telephone, were there any other devices for -- any other communication devices?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think there were, yes. I often heard, in the evening, people talking loudly, and there was a sort of radio station or something like that. Radio transmitter, something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: You said yesterday that Mr. Meakic sent you to the restaurant together with the person you knew who was brought in together with you, Joachim [sic], to the pista; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: Ibrahim. I apologise. Ibrahim. As we're discussing the time you spent in the restaurant, could you tell the Trial Chamber how much time during the day you spent in the restaurant?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: With respect to the time I spent in Omarska and in the restaurant itself, it was not us that made the decision. A guard would come to escort us to the restaurant. That was in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: What time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that it was round about 7.00 or 8.00 or half past 7.00, and sometimes we were there until 7.00 or 8.00, sometimes longer. We would wait for orders. We waited to be told that we had completed our work and that we would go back to our room, always escorted by a guard. We were not able to walk around on our own.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: Let us go back to the room that you entered the first time you arrived. During the time you spent in the restaurant, did you know -- did you happen to know what that premises was used for?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean the reception office. The reception office. Why, for work in the concentration camp. That's where the prisoners were taken to. That's where all the paperwork was done. There was a lot of paper there and records would be kept. The personnel would be distributed around the camp, the people working in the camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: Witness, I am asking you whether from the restaurant where you were and the time that you described to us so nicely, did you happen to see what was -- who was working in the room and what was going on in the room?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: Did typists come to the camp with the investigators and interrogators?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: Do you know their names?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: Who were they?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: Slavica Lakic; Nena, I don't know her surname, I know her by sight; and Nada Markovski. They were all employees of the SUP, the centre of public security, before the war as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: They spent the whole time there with the investigators, according to you the interrogators, in that room on the upper floor?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I saw them come to work together, and they would leave together.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: You were there for over 50 days. Do you have any information, that is to say, did you see or hear in which rooms Mrs. Lakic, Ms. Markovski, and I think it was Ms. Nena Sikman, where they were?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see with my own eyes the rooms in which they worked.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: So you don't know which room they worked in?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not know exactly, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us now go back to the restaurant. In order to save time, be brief, please. What was the working day like of the women prisoners? What was their day like?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, it was compulsory labour, as far as I was concerned. A guard would come to take us off in the morning, and he would say, "You're going downstairs." This would be about 7.00, 7.30, perhaps even 6.30 on occasion. We would go down to the restaurant, us women, the women who were put up in two rooms on the upper floor, and I would then wait for the guard to issue orders and tell us what we were going to do that day. Usually one group of women, on any particular day, would give out the one meal per day to the prisoners, whereas another group of women, on orders from the guards, would wash the lavatories on the floor above. This occurred very often. We would usually have to clean the bathroom and rather a big room where there were a lot of tables and chairs, and I could only assume that meetings were held there because I was assigned to do cleaning work there once. We would wash the floors, and we would do everything we were asked to do or, that is to say, ordered to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: Witness J --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: And this would go on throughout the whole day.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: Witness, in view of your experience, could you try and focus on answering my questions. But as you have already broached the subject, let me ask you the following: The women cleaned the premises on the upper floor while the investigators were working?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sometimes. Sometimes. Usually it was the bathroom, the toilet, and this sort of big room like a conference hall. Sometimes. Not all the time. Usually we would be working within the frameworks of the restaurant. We would clean the restaurant, serve the meal, clear the dishes away, wash the dishes, and sometimes we would go into another section, which was known as the separation plant, and work there too.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: We'll come to that, Witness, all in good time. Was there a table where the women would sit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there was. As you enter the restaurant, in the left-hand corner there was a small table with several chairs. We weren't all able to sit down. Some of us would sit on the radiator.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: For me to be able to understand you better -- you mentioned the corner. Now, is that corner nearer to the pista or was it the corner next to the point where the meal was handed out?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: When was the food given out usually?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sometimes nine, sometimes ten, sometimes later, because the food wasn't actually prepared there. It wasn't cooked there. It was brought to the restaurant from the separation plant. We would just serve the food at the counter.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: Now, the process of serving the food, was it -- was there a lot of commotion, comings and goings, people coming in, people going out?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: The people would come in, in groups, depending on how the guards distributed them, but they would come in for meals in groups. They would start at 8.00 or 9.00. Sometimes the food would be late, so it would go on into the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: But I'm interested in the distribution process.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: We would stand at the counter where the meals were given out. We would put the food in the plates.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: So a group of people would come in; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: They would sit down?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: They would get up?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: And there was this constant motion?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. Sometimes the guards would say, "Stop, Wait." But you had two to three minutes to eat your meal. If you failed to do so during that time, you would be beaten up in the restaurant.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: We'll come to that, Witness, as well.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: I just don't want to forget anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: Very well. You won't forget. Now, in this process of food distribution and the involvement of the women, some of the women would hand out the food, the others would be washing dishes, and this mass of people moving around. How far were you able to see what was actually happening outside the restaurant and which women were outside, which were inside the restaurant?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I could see because the restaurant was -- the walls of the restaurant were glass. There were glass partitions, and if you stood at the counter handing out the food, you had a clear vision of the "white house" and the pista. While you were waiting for an order, you could see glass -- you could see everything. You could see glass -- there was glass around you. You could see the cries of people. You could see the people being beaten in front of your very eyes and falling down in the restaurant. I could see everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: Witness, we spoke a moment ago about the people coming in, going out, moving around.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were running, they weren't standing. They were entering at great speed because they were in a panic whether they could eat the meal in the time allotted them.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: I am just asking you whether this mass of people influenced your vision in any way.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. And I state clearly it did not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Keegan.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, there is a distinct difference between asking questions and allowing the witness to answer and being argumentative. I have been trying to be lenient with this, but it has reached the stage now where counsel is simply arguing with the witness. He's asking questions, she's attempting to answer, and he then begins to argue if he doesn't like the answer. I would like counsel admonished to simply ask the questions and allow counsel -- the witness to answer, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Simic, your response, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation], Your Honour, the questions were quite clear. I did not even ask the lady about this separation plant because I have information of who issued orders. My questions are clear, but the lady is giving answers which have nothing to do with my questions, so I have to stop her when she does so. I would just like to have the witness answer my questions without drawing attention away from my actual questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Krstan Simic, on condition that you ask your questions in a clear manner. It is not clear if you say, for example, what does a workday -- what was a workday like? That is not a clear question. What does it resemble? What does it look like? Does it look like a person, an event? Be more precise. It is up to -- otherwise, you'll get the witness describing the whole day and telling you what it looks like. And that is one -- and there's another point I would like to insist upon. Ask questions; don't enter into arguments with the witness. Ask the witness a question, and accept the answer you are given. If your question is a clear one, you will have a clear answer; or if not, repeat it several times. So I insist upon this example. It is not -- you're not asking a clear question if you ask her what her working day was like. That's not a clear-cut question. So please try and ask your questions clearly and don't enter into arguments with the witness. If you are satisfied with the answer, perhaps you could give the witness a sign to stop; but if you enter into this kind of dialogue, as you know, we have a difficult time following, and so do the interpreters. So you can make a sign with your hand, and I think that the witness will understand that you mean her to stop. Having said that, Mr. Simic, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: A moment ago you confirmed -- you said to Mr. O'Sullivan that you spoke about the events in Omarska truthfully; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: During your talk with the investigators and the representatives of the OTP, you said on one occasion that you -- that from the prisoners, the name was deleted, whether it was a she or he, that you heard from one of the prisoners that Mr. Zeljko Meakic had said that the Crisis Staff of the Prijedor municipality decided upon all questions related to the camp, having to do with the camp, including how long the prisoners are required to stay in the camp. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: Bearing in mind your education and professional training, and Mr. Keegan referred to that frequently yesterday, I should like to ask you to take a look at a document which the usher is now going to show you, and I ask the usher to present D17/1, and D/1A, the English and B/C/S version. D17/1, and D17/1A. Witness J, would you read through the document carefully.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean the whole document?

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, the complete document. Have you read it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I have not. I need a little more time.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: Please take your time.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: Witness J, would you please focus on the introduction of this order. Was this order -- the chief of the public security station of Prijedor on the 31st of May, 1992, did he issue this order in keeping with a decision taken by the Crisis Staff of the Prijedor municipality?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: Does that stem from this order?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: I read through it fairly quickly, and I really couldn't comment. This would require a greater study on my part. I see that it was signed by the chief; I see at the top it says that it is the decision of the Crisis Staff; but other than that, I can't comment.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: Very well, then I'll ask you to read point number two, if you will.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Mr. Krstan Simic, but do you need to ask the witness to read a part of the document? Why don't you go ahead and ask the question that you want to ask, because the witness has read the document. Why ask her to read it again? Because you run the risk of having the witness repeating this -- of having to read it two or three times. I think that it would be preferable if you were to go ahead and ask your question, and if the witness needs to reread the document or portionings of it, she will do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the witness, asked by my learned colleague Mr. Keegan yesterday, talked about the structure and the organisation of the camp, and we now want to go through those questions. I accept your suggestion, of course, if the witness is ready to follow me and follow my questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. That would be preferable. Otherwise, we're going to waste a lot of time, Mr. Simic. But I don't want to tell you how to do your work. The essential point is to be clear and to organise our work in such a manner that it would perhaps be better to ask the witness the question, having already taken the time she needed to read the document. Then she won't have to read the document again. That is just a suggestion on my part, but go ahead. The floor is yours.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I accept your proposal. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: In point 2 of the order, it says that persons who have been taken into custody with the documents they have should be turned over to the leader of security, who is duty-bound, in cooperation with the coordinators of the service of national, public, and military security to place these persons into one of five set rooms which are provided for the accommodation of persons taken into custody. Did Mr. Meakic put you up in the restaurant in keeping with this decision?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: He told the guard to take me to the restaurant and that I was to wait there for my name to be called out to go for interrogation.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: I stated that clearly yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: You spoke about interrogations and investigations.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, whichever word you like to use.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: And the structure and organisation of the police. I should now like to draw your attention to point 3, which states the following: "Investigations are carried out under the guidance of Mirko Misic from the state security system; Ranko Mijic, the head of the criminological department of the public security station of Prijedor; and Lieutenant-Colonel Majstorovic in charge of military security." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: Point 6, and the order contains the following: "That security of this institutional camp be provided by the police station of Omarska." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: A moment ago, you said that the food was prepared outside the camp and was brought into the camp, to the restaurant. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: I'd now like to draw your attention to provision 7 of this order, which states the following: It says that the mine administration is duty-bound to organise food for the investigators, the guards, and all prisoners, and to organise the cleaning of the compound and the installations linked to the work of the compound.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Krstan Simic, I apologise for interrupting you again. I have a question to ask you at this point -- to ask the witness about this point. Witness, did you know -- before arriving in the Omarska camp, did you know about this document?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I am seeing this document for the first time here today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You mean today? You've seen the document for the first time today?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. When the Defence counsel handed me this document, that is the first time I see it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Simic, this brings us to another question. We very often talk about equality and striking a balance between all parties. The observations and the answers made by the witness to the questions put to her by the Prosecutor were exclusively based on what she saw in the camp; that is to say, the conclusions that the witness drew with respect to the camp's organisation were drawn exclusively on the basis of her observations. Therefore, your questions should also be based on this foundation, otherwise, you are going to enter into a process of argumentativeness with the witness; that is to say, if you say, "You noticed that. You observed that." But if this was observed on the basis of a document -- you asked whether there was on the basis of a document, and the witness answered that she had not seen this before going to Omarska. She said she saw the document here for the first time today. Therefore, Mr. Krstan Simic, in order to strike a balance -- strike the proper balance between all parties, you must ask your questions on the basis of what the witness observed, and, that is to say, the sources on which the witness gave her answers to the Prosecutor. Am I making myself clear?

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, you have been clear. With all due respect, I wish to stress that the Prosecution, yesterday -- but we failed to react -- but at least on 20 occasions -- we went through the transcript -- the Prosecution used the education and experience of this present witness in order to obtain certain information linked to organisational matters with respect to the organisation of the police for state security, investigation and interrogation, and it was only on the basis of the principle of equality did we adopt this method, and that is why I said using her experience, we wish to arrive at the truth, and we will be raising questions which the witness will be able to answer on the basis of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Simic, I completely agree with you on that point. The Prosecutor did ask questions, yes, on the basis of the database that the witness had and her observations. There we agree. However, as you know full well, this document was not entered; that is to say, the witness did not have knowledge of it beforehand. And the questions that you are asking, I accept them. You are authorised to ask the witness questions on the organisation of the camp, that is true. Indeed it is. You do have this right. But you must ask these questions on the same basis that the Prosecutor did, have the same groundwork and foundations, that is to say, the knowledge that the witness has through her legal training and the results of her observations during the time she spent in the camp. That means that you do not have the right to use a document which the witness has never seen before. Thus the answers that she gave to the Prosecutor were not based upon a document which the witness had never seen before. It is a question of logic. You do have the right to ask questions. Yes, you do. But only if you use the same database, so to speak. In my opinion, that is quite clear. So please go ahead. Ask your questions but without utilising the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: Witness J, who was in charge of preparing the food for the detainees?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see who it was. The food would arrive ready-made, and I don't know who prepared the food.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Krstan Simic, I just want to say that it was a good question. One also has to compliment you when you ask the right question in a proper manner.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, allow me to say just one sentence. I had in front of me a rather banal legal document for which one doesn't need any special expertise or experience, and in view of the principle adopted by my learned colleague, I just wanted the Witness J to give us her interpretation of the document. She obviously doesn't wish to do so, so we're not going to pursue the issue. That was my intent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Keegan.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I must confess we were waiting for what we thought was going to be the foundation -- end of the foundational questions. The document is clear on its face. The question for this witness would be, obviously: "Were you aware that the mine company was responsible for preparing the food based on an order? Were you aware of this? Were you aware of that?" Either she is or she's not. But the document, one, we don't believe requires any interpretation; and two, if that's what he's seeking to do, then again we believe that pursuant to the amendments in the Rules, he is now well beyond the scope of cross-examination. This has nothing to do with the credibility of the witness or the information elicited directly on our examination, and, therefore, he is now taking this witness as his own witness. He's now calling this witness and should be conducting a direct examination with respect to this order if he believes it needs interpretation. And then in that instance, he should so advise the Chamber and the Prosecution so that we can then prepare ourselves for cross-examination if we felt it was necessary. It's a question of what's he's trying to elicit from the witness, and if what he's trying to do is see if she had knowledge that affects what she said yesterday, then that should be the question, "Are you aware?" Not a simple diatribe about the document, which is clear on its face.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Simic, how do you respond to that? The Prosecutor has advanced an objection. Do you wish to respond that objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. Thank you for giving me this opportunity. It is true that this portion of the examination is relevant to both parties of the case. This is going to be the topic of some other evidence, and I do not wish to waste any more time on that. Witness J indeed spoke about the organisation of the camp, and we wanted to clear the issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes, of course, Mr. Simic. We're not going to dwell on the issue any longer. We do not disagree with that. We are very well aware of the fact that the witness spoke about the organisation of the camp, and we agree with your approach in principle. However, I wanted to warn you about the proper way of asking your questions. So the right question should begin with saying, "You told the Prosecutor so and so." It seems that Mr. O'Sullivan wishes to add something to the discussion.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: I wish to say something for the record, Your Honour, and it's not to do with this particular witness, but for the record, I submit that the submissions made by my learned friend about scope of cross-examination I would disagree with. So I want to make it clear that should it arise at a later time about whose witness this is and cross-examination, or somehow this witness becomes the other party's witness, and the scope of Rule 90, for the record, I would disagree with my friend. I just want to lay down that marker.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but we all know that if we follow the rules, we don't have any problem. It is only when one tries to go beyond the scope of the regulations that we have a problem. The witness spoke about the organisational aspect of the camp. I have already stated that I agree with that. But your question should perhaps begin, "You told to the Prosecutor that," et cetera, and on the basis of that, you can proceed with the actual question.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: Witness J, do you know to whom Mr. Meakic reported concerning his work?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I do not.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: Witness J, do you know about Mr. Mirko Jesic who was the coordinator for the public security affairs? Do you know to whom he submitted his reports?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I do not.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: Witness J, do you know to whom Mr. -- Colonel Majstorovic, who was in charge of military security affairs, submitted his reports?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I do not.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: And what about Mr. Meakic, do you know to whom he submitted his reports?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I can only guess.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: Very well, then, you don't know. Yesterday you spoke about the organisation of the police in the Prijedor municipality; however, a number of things remained unclear. I'm referring to the period of 1992. Is it true that in the area of the Prijedor municipality, the police was organised in stations, public security stations, and did it constitute a SUP or public security station on its own?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: As regards the public security station in question, there were two sectors, a sectors for public security and another one, sector, for state security; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: As regards the public security sector, were there any police stations that were part of that sector?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: As regards the relevant period of time, the year of 1992, was there a single police station in Prijedor which had a general jurisdiction with three special departments, one in Kozarac, one in Ljubija, and one in Omarska; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: As regards the public security sector in the area of Prijedor, was there a special station which was in charge of traffic control?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there was.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: Let me go back to the police station which had general jurisdiction over the area and which was composed of three separate departments. Did those departments constitute the lowest organisational level within the whole structure?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: It may have been the case, but I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: You mentioned Mr. Meakic yesterday on several occasions.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: Did you know about his position within the Omarska police station before the camp, the unfortunate camp was set up?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: What was his position?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was a police commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: So he was the police commander of the Omarska police station?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is what I heard, but I never went there myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: Witness J, let me now remind you of the statement that you gave to the investigators of the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us give a copy of the statement to the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: Shall I give you back the previous document?

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, please. Thank you. Witness J, you have told us about the statement, the circumstances of the statement that you gave to Ms. Hollis and other investigators of the Tribunal. Let me turn your attention to page 4. It's the same page in the English version, the fourth paragraph. "Zeljko Meakic, who was the camp commander or camp manager. I say camp commander or camp manager because the guards referred to him as the person in charge and acted toward him as though he were the man in charge. I heard him issue commands to the guards, he acted as the boss of the guards. There was a young guard who would come to our sleeping room and bother Namka. He was often drunk. Once I heard Zeljko Meakic tell this young guard to report to him, and that the guard could not drink while he was on duty." Is that correct, Witness?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: In this statement and the contacts that you had with the representatives of the OTP, you mentioned Mr. Drasko Zec, Zivko Dragosavljevic, Milenko Tomcic, Slavko Bereta, and Dragan Radetic, also known as Draja; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: You also said that on one occasion, Mr. Zec told you that the gentlemen that I have just named were given cases and files from the president of the Tribunal who, in turn, had received them from Mr. Drljaca. I'm referring to the cases involving individuals to be interrogated.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot see that in the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: I have another statement which contains that piece of information. I just want to know if this is correct.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: As regards Mr. Drljaca, is that the same person who issued the order?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean who signed the order?

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, who signed the order.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: Who was Mr. Drasko Zec?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: (redacted)

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: (redacted)

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: (redacted)

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and there was a lawyer whom you didn't mention.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: Witness J, Mr. Meakic, whom you referred to as a police station commander, could he issue orders to Mr. Zec, Mr. Tomcic, and Mr. Dragosavljevic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: On the basis of your education, of your professional education, was it possible for a low-level police commander to issue orders to a Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: The times were not logical. I don't know whether he was able to issue him orders or not. I believe I was clear enough in my response.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: Did you ever see Mr. Meakic issue an order to Mr. Milenko Tomcic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: Did you ever see him issue an order to Mr. Zec?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: Did you ever see him issue any order to anyone from the law enforcement organs?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: We spoke about Mr. Mijic --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: -- who was the chief of the crime department of the police station of Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: Was he a highly-ranking official within the public security station?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: Did you ever see Mr. Meakic issue an order to Mr. Mijic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: Witness J, did you ever see Mr. Meakic issue any order to Mr. Jesic who was with the statement security department?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know Mr. Jesic very well, but, no, I don't know him.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: How about Lieutenant Colonel Majstorovic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know Lieutenant Colonel Majstorovic either.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: Were you ever able to see Mr. Meakic issue orders to the interrogators?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Were you ever in a position to see Mr. Kvocka issue any order to any of the individuals that I have mentioned?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the individuals that you have mentioned a moment ago?

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: Have you -- did you ever see Momcilo Gruban issue any orders to the individuals mentioned?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Yesterday you told us on several occasions that Mr. Meakic was the commander and that Mr. Kvocka was the deputy; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: You were also very clear when you said that the war assignment of Mr. Kvocka and Mr. Meakic was such that when Mr. Meakic was absent, Mr. Kvocka would take over. Is that a correct piece of information as well?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: More or less. That is what usually happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: Witness J, I will again have to refer you to your statement, page 5, paragraph 2. "I would say that Meakic was always in the camp. He was always there during the day and often in the night. He would be in the office to which I was first taken, or making tours around the camp." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Likewise, yesterday you spoke about the orders of Mr. Meakic and Mr. Kvocka to the guards. You said that they would give them their assignments involving their guard duty. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: As regards the guards in particular, would they receive on a daily basis the assignments, that is, the exact positions that they were supposed to stand guard?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't remember that very precisely, but I was very often present during those occasions when the assignments were given to the guards.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Simic, I'm sorry to interrupt you, but just tell us how much time you think you will need to finish your cross-examination. I think we will all soon need a break. We are all rather tired at this point.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have quite a few questions, Your Honour, quite a few.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us have a half-hour break, then, at this point. Mr. Usher, please, could you please first help the witness out of the courtroom. Witness J, would you stay put for a while, please. We shall come back at around five minutes to one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please be seated. Mr. Simic, we're ready. You may continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: Witness J, yesterday and today, on several occasions, you spoke about the time that shifts were taking place, the shifts of the security personnel. So without repeating, I should like to ask you the following: Where were the shifts relieved and replaced? Where was this official takeover of duty and change of shifts of guards?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: Usually it was in front of the restaurant, and I was able to see this; that is to say, in the vicinity of the restaurant, the pista.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: On the pista.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Yesterday and today, you repeated that you had occasion to see Mr. Meakic issue orders to the security personnel when they were receiving their daily assignments, where they would be on duty, in fact, in the camp. What was the role of Mr. Kvocka in those orders?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: He also issued orders and assigned the guards and went on tour of the camp with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: Did he do so in the presence of Mr. Meakic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would see him alone.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Yesterday you testified and mentioned an individual named Mirko Babic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: I should like to ask you now to take a look at your statement again, and it is page 9 of your statement, the beginning of the page, and I quote: "I often saw, during the day but most often at night, at the camp Mirko Babic. I saw him often at night on the first floor. He was not a guard. He was an engineer. He told us women that he worked as the supervisor of the mine as his work obligation, duty." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He told us that.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: You also state in that same paragraph: "He would sometimes come to the restaurant and say that someone had to go to the Separacija the next day and clean it and tell us to decide who would go." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: Can you explain to the Court, please, what is meant by "work duty" or "work obligation" in the kind of system that we lived and worked in?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have used mild terms to express myself here in this statement. I say that now -- I say now that it was forced labour. The work duty was that you had to do what your superior ordered you to do, ordered.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: Witness, I was not speaking about your own obligation or work duty, but I was talking about the work duty of Mr. Babic. You needn't answer if you cannot.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am speaking about the time during the camp. I'm not talking about what "work duty" meant before that. That's not essential here.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: The military conscripts in the system of total national defence, All People's Defence, did they have either a military obligation to do Civil Defence work or a work duty of some kind? Is that correct? Would you say that that was right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: According to Mr. Babic's statement, the engineer who worked in the company, he was performing his work obligation or duty in the Omarska mine; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what he told us, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In addition to Mr. Babic, were there any other people, let me use the term "civilians," like cleaning ladies, for example, who did work of any kind?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: Witness J, in addition to these cleaning ladies, were there any other civilians working on maintenance for the water and pump system or people who drove that unfortunate yellow TAM truck or anything of that kind?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: So they were the workers or employees of the mining company of Omarska; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I didn't know them beforehand. I don't know what kind of work they did before that.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: Mr. Babic himself, did he supervise the work of the maintenance men, seeing to the maintenance of the pumps and so on, pumping devices?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know. I really can't say.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You told Mr. O'Sullivan today in detail about the length of the statements given to Ms. Hollis, how long you took to make the statements, that it lasted for a period of two days, and that you spoke about the events that were uppermost in your mind; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: I should like to go back to one particular event which you brought up yesterday during your testimony, and that is the injury of Ms. Besirevic in Buk Bijela.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: I apologise. Ms. Besirevic, Mugbila Besirevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: There was something that was not quite clear in the transcript, so I should like to ask you to describe the event once again, please, the --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very well. I said yesterday that one day a man came to the restaurant whom I had not seen in the camp beforehand. I did not notice that he was a guard or did anything there. He came up to me -- he came up to the table, that is to say. He came up to the table that Mugbila Besirevic was sitting at, and it was the table that I mentioned that existed in the restaurant itself today. He shouted at her. He abused her and accused her of having to do with some computers, allegedly, as she was a bank employee in the bank in Prijedor, that she had sent something to the Muslims of Cazinska Krajina or something like that, and he was shouting at her that she had used the computers to perform this transaction. He took out a knife, and on his [sic] face cut in the sign of a cross, and blood flowed from her face. Mugbila was turned to stone. I saw that with my very eyes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: On her face, not on his face, I apologise.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: None of the guards who were present in the restaurant or who were around the restaurant reacted to this event. I apologise, but I have to say that Mugbila is no longer among the living.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: I'm very sorry to hear that, Witness. Witness J, this image, this occurrence, what effect did it have on you and the rest of the women?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were in a state of shock. We were absolutely petrified and glued to the spot.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us the time that this took place in the restaurant?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was during my stay. Perhaps it was July. I cannot tell you more certainly than that. It was daylight.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: Was food being handed out at the time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot remember because there was usually a break in the distribution of food; perhaps we had to wait for more food to be brought in. But at any rate, it was in the course of the day.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: Among everything that you experienced during your stay, is this the worst incident that you witnessed in view of the fact what it took place in the place you were, very close to you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Lots of things went on in the camp. There were many things like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: During your two days of conversation with Ms. Hollis, you never mentioned that event, that is to say, you never mentioned it, brought it up before you entered the court here yesterday.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that I didn't have enough time, and whenever I speak of occurrences of that kind and the time I spent there, I never have enough time. And if Mr. Keegan were to ask me something today, I would not have enough time to answer him, and there might be something that I have missed because in the two terrible months that I spent there, to recount all that in the space of a couple of pages or a few hours, that is not long enough for me to be able to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Keegan.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I object 'cause that is a direct misrepresentation of the facts. Counsel has the statements in front of him. If he looks on page 14 in the English, that incident is very clearly described. It's obvious that giving testimony here is difficult enough for these witnesses, and I believe that counsel is engaged in a direct pattern to try and confuse this witness, and we object, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Krstan Simic, your response.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, in the Bosnian version, that detail is -- does not exist; but my colleague says that in the English version on page 14, it says that Ms. Mugbila was cut by -- that there was a kokarda in question, because the cutting with a knife or with a kokarda is not the same thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. But the witness has already said -- answered several times. She said several times that she did not have sufficient time to recount all the events that had taken place. And we're all professionals here, and we can do the experiment here in the courtroom. You can ask one thing one day, and you'll get one answer; you can ask the same thing another day, and you will not get the same answer. We are all professionals, and we know that kind of thing happens. So please continue with your work, and bear in mind the fact that the witness has already answered, Mr. Krstan Simic.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: And to end with the injury of the unfortunate Mugbila, could you describe to us in precise terms where the injury was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: On her cheek.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Yesterday on several occasions --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Keegan.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, just for the record, I want to make it clear that on page 14, in the third paragraph in the Bosnian version, this incident is recounted where a man wearing a kokarda came in and cut Mugbila on the cheek and accused her of stealing something with computers. So it's in both versions, and it's clear, and we object to the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Chamber regrets all these incidents which are making us lose a lot of time, and as we haven't got the document, we can't see it. But anyway, please continue, Mr. Simic.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: Witness J, yesterday during your testimony, you said that you saw Mr. Kvocka, Mr. Prcac, and Krkan attending the beating -- attending beatings, that they were present during beatings; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: Can you describe an event of this kind and the victims, the time it took place and the manner in which it took place? We're all professionals here, as our Judge rightly noted, so we'll be able to judge.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: Everything that happened in the camp they saw. They passed by bodies. They moved around the camp compound. They saw what the guards were doing. So for me, there is no dilemma there. The names of the individuals who were tortured when they passed I don't know. I can't give you their names.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: Witness J, you say they saw everything, and I am asking you to recount what -- any one event that they witnessed.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dead people thrown in front of the "white house" next to the fence, they would pass by that way. Is that enough? Is that sufficient for you?

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: I haven't got the answer that my question asked you about.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: They moved around, passed by dead bodies that were in their path.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: Well, as my colleague Mr. Fila would say, I suppose that is an answer, too, yes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: They saw dead people being loaded up onto trucks.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: Witness J, yesterday during your testimony before this Trial Chamber, you said that you drank water in the camp that was prohibited for drinking, that it was not potable water.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what the guards told us. The guards told us that it was water for industrial purposes, for the purification of iron ore.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: Do you know which organ issued this decree that water -- that the water should not be drunk, that it was not potable water? Do you know who issued that decree?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: The water that you drank can be -- we can test it to see whether it is drinkable, potable water or not; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but the guards did not drink that same water. The guards and the personnel drank other water. Other water was brought in for them in canisters, in jerrycans.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You also spoke about one particular incident yesterday which I would like to refer to now. You spoke yesterday about the 10th of June, the day -- the first day after your arrival in Omarska and the event that Mr. Zigic took part in; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: You said that this was observed by Mr. Meakic and Mr. Kvocka; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Radic was in the camp on that day too. When I went back to my room, he was sitting down in his office.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: Did you see Radic within Zigic's area of vision?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember, but I remember seeing him in the office when we came back from our work duties.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: Witness J, can you tell me when this was in the course of the day, or perhaps the time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was sometime during the afternoon. I can't give you the exact time.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: I should like to ask you to look at a photograph which the usher will show you.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Would the usher kindly take up the photograph, and a copy for the Prosecution, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: Witness J, you have before you the restaurant, the entrance to the administration building, and the area that was referred to as the pista; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: Can you indicate and draw the position you were in at that moment?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: You want me to do this straight away?

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: Perhaps the document could be placed on the ELMO and then you could do that there.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was here, right there. That's where the radiator was, and we were sitting around there.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
